title: Toroca to the Common Grave: the Amazona of the Republiquetas and the War for Upper Peru
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Toroca, the Convent, and the House of Padilla

stops.name: Toroca, birth in the hacienda lands above Chuquisaca
stops.campa: In the hacienda lands of Toroca, in the hills above Chuquisaca, a daughter is born on 12 July 1780 to the landowner Matías Azurduy, criollo of Basque stock, and his wife Eulalia Bermúdez, a chola of Chuquisaca: Juana. From infancy the girl moves between tongues that are not Spanish, Quechua and Aymara, learned at the fires of the tenant families who work her father's fields. He teaches her to ride and to shoot, skills a hacendado's daughter does not commonly receive, and she takes to both as if the horse and the gun were owed to her.
suggested_refs: The Argentine 10-peso banknote bearing her imagined portrait, minted two centuries after this birth

stops.name: Chuquisaca, orphaned
stops.campa: Juana is seven when her mother's heart fails her suddenly in the family house at Chuquisaca. Her father does not long outlive her: within the same span of years he too is dead, by the account the family keeps, murdered by a nobleman whose name the chronicle withholds, over a matter never made public. The two orphaned sisters, Juana and the younger Rosalía, pass into the keeping of an aunt and uncle, Petrona Azurduy and Francisco Díaz Valle, who raise them by the rule of catechism and obedience rather than the freedom of Toroca's open fields.
suggested_refs: The Azurduy family house in Chuquisaca, now vanished into the modern city

stops.name: Convento de Santa Teresa, the enclosure
stops.campa: To settle a dispute over her guardianship and her small inheritance, the family places sixteen-year-old Juana within the walls of the Convento de Santa Teresa in Chuquisaca, the strictest Carmelite house in Upper Peru. She learns embroidery, the psalter, the discipline of silence between offices. But the girl who was taught to ride and to shoot chafes against the grille; she gathers the younger novices to read by candle-stub what the house forbids, the rebellion of Túpac Amaru, the verses of Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, and argues the enclosure's rules openly with the mother superior.
suggested_refs: The Convento de Santa Teresa, Sucre, now the Museo de Santa Clara / Santa Teresa

stops.name: Convento de Santa Teresa, the expulsion
stops.campa: After eight months the mother superior has had enough of her. The clandestine readings, the arguments over the rule, the refusal to be made quiet: the convent expels Juana at seventeen and sends her back to Toroca with her dowry unspent and her marriageability, by the city's reckoning, in question. She rides home unbothered by the verdict. What the sisters could not tame in her is the same restlessness that will, within thirty years, be called by the government of Buenos Aires a lieutenant colonelcy, and by the people of two republics a legend.
suggested_refs: The Convento de Santa Teresa's enclosure grille, Sucre

stops.name: Toroca, the neighbor Manuel Ascencio Padilla
stops.campa: Back at her father's hacienda, Juana falls into the company of Manuel Ascencio Padilla, son of the neighboring hacendado Melchor Padilla and a law student at Chuquisaca's university. Manuel had stood in the crowd that watched the cacique Dámaso Catari executed by the colonial court, and the sight never left him. Between the two young people passes a courtship built on borrowed books: Rousseau, the Encyclopédie, the new grammar of liberty circulating in manuscript among educated colonials who have never seen Paris. They find in each other a rare thing, a marriage of equal appetite for the coming war.
suggested_refs: Manuel Ascencio Padilla's law studies at the Universidad Real y Pontificia de San Francisco Xavier, Chuquisaca

stops.name: Toroca, marriage to Manuel Ascencio Padilla
stops.campa: At twenty-five Juana marries Manuel Ascencio Padilla in the parish of her home country, a match the neighborhood calls sensible and the two of them privately call something larger. Padilla stands beside his wife, on the hacienda and later on the battlefield, in a way the age does not expect of husbands; five children will be born to them in the years that follow, Manuel, Mariano, Juliana, Mercedes, and Luisa, none of them born into a house that will ever again know an ordinary peace. The war that will take four of the five is only four years off.
suggested_refs: The parish marriage register of Toroca, Chuquisaca

stops.name: Chuquisaca, the Revolution of 25 May
stops.campa: The Real Audiencia of Charcas rises against its president, Ramón García de León y Pizarro, on 25 May 1809, the first cry of the whole continent's independence, months ahead of Buenos Aires and Caracas. Juana and Manuel, four years married, join the tumult in Chuquisaca's streets; Padilla is marked among the leading conspirators. Within months the counter-revolution, led by General Goyeneche, executes the movement's chiefs and hunts the rest. Padilla flees south into the hills, sheltered village by village by indigenous families who owe him nothing but choose him anyway. The war that will consume them both begins here.
suggested_refs: Casa de la Libertad, Sucre, seat of the Real Audiencia of Charcas

stops.name: Cochabamba, the uprising of 14 September
stops.campa: Word of Buenos Aires's May Revolution reaches Upper Peru, and Cochabamba rises in turn on 14 September 1810. Padilla, hunted since Chuquisaca's fall, enlists under the rebel commander Esteban Arce, given command of two thousand indigenous fighters posted to cut the royal supply road between Lagunillas and Chuquisaca. Juana, hidden with her small children in a succession of safe hamlets, has not yet taken the field herself; she keeps house in secret while her husband's name becomes one the royalist governors circulate on their wanted lists, a debt they mean to collect from his family if not from him.
suggested_refs: The Cochabamba uprising of 1810, precursor to the Batallas de las Heroínas of 1812

stops.name: Tarabuco, the arrest and the rescue by night
stops.campa: The net closes after Cochabamba falls. Royalist soldiers seize what remains of the Padilla and Azurduy lands and take Juana and her children as surety against the fugitive husband. Manuel comes by night to the guardhouse near Tarabuco with three horses and cuts the sentries down himself, freeing his wife and sons in the dark before the alarm can carry. From this hour there is no hacienda left to return to, only the hills; the family lives now as its enemies already assume it lives, hidden, moving, armed, a household with no roof but the republiqueta still to be founded.
suggested_refs: The heights above Tarabuco, staging ground of the family's flight

stops.name: Guaqui, the disaster on the shore of Titicaca
stops.campa: On the reed-fringed shore of Lake Titicaca, at Guaqui, the First Auxiliary Expedition sent from Buenos Aires is broken by the royalist army of Goyeneche on 20 June 1811. The news reaches the hunted families of Chuquisaca province like a second sentence: the army that was to relieve Upper Peru has been erased in an afternoon, and the whole territory falls back under the Crown for a season. For Juana and Manuel, in hiding above Tarabuco, Guaqui means only this, that no help is coming from the south, and that the war they are already living has no near end.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Guaqui (Huaqui), on the Bolivian shore of Titicaca

stops.name: La Laguna, the republiqueta begins
stops.campa: In the broken country north of Chuquisaca, among the ranges the country calls Carretas, Sombreros, and Mandinga, Manuel Ascencio Padilla plants the standard of a guerrilla state that answers to no viceroy and, for now, to no Buenos Aires either: the Republiqueta de La Laguna, seated in the town of the same name. From Presto to Tomina to Pomabamba the villages of the department declare for him. Juana is at his side, no longer merely the fugitive's wife but a co-founder of the territory, learning the country's ravines and passes as a general learns a map, because she will soon have to command in them.
suggested_refs: The Republiqueta de La Laguna, one of the longest-lived guerrilla republics of the independence wars

stops.name: La Laguna, Juana's apprenticeship of arms
stops.campa: While Manuel rides the republiqueta's circuit, Juana stays at the camp of La Laguna with the children and begins, in secret at first, to make herself a soldier: she sets up straw effigies at the camp's edge and practices with the boleadoras and the lance until her arm no longer tires. Word comes of the women of Cochabamba who threw themselves against Goyeneche's advance with stones and kitchen knives rather than surrender their hill. Between that example and the danger closing on the mountain camp, Juana decides what she has been circling toward since the convent: she will not wait at the fire. She will ride.
suggested_refs: The Batallas de las Heroínas de la Coronilla, Cochabamba, 27 May 1812, the women's stand that steels her resolve

stops.name: La Laguna, Juan Huallparrimachi joins the household
stops.campa: A cholo youth of uncommon gift comes into the Padilla camp: Juan Huallparrimachi, natural son of the former governor of Potosí, Francisco de Paula Sanz, and an indigenous mother, a poet in Quechua and a born soldier both. Manuel makes him lieutenant; Juana, childless in her heart for the sons she has had to hide away with distant caretakers, treats him as her own. He trains her boys in bow and lance and huaraca when he can reach them, scouts the royalist columns, and becomes within months indispensable to the republiqueta's survival, the nearest thing to a fourth Padilla child the war allows her to raise.
suggested_refs: Juan Huallparrimachi's Quechua verses, among the earliest indigenous-language poetry of the independence wars

stops.name: Jujuy, the Éxodo Jujeño
stops.campa: As Belgrano empties Jujuy before the royalist advance, ordering the whole province south in a single column of carts, cattle, and refugees and burning what cannot be carried, the guerrillas of the republiquetas harry the Spanish rear from the north, buying the retreating army its margin. Padilla's riders strike supply trains and isolated pickets across the puna; Juana organizes the camp's stores and its wounded, unseen by Belgrano's staff but already known by name to the officers who pass word up the line that a woman commands alongside Padilla in Upper Peru, and commands well.
suggested_refs: The Éxodo Jujeño monument, San Salvador de Jujuy

stops.name: Potosí, reunion under Belgrano's banner
stops.campa: Belgrano's Second Auxiliary Expedition enters Potosí in triumph after Salta and Tucumán, and here, after long separation, Juana and Manuel present themselves and their irregulars to the general's headquarters in the Villa Imperial. Belgrano, who values discipline as much as courage, is struck by the ten thousand indigenous militia the Padillas can call to arms on the strength of reputation alone, and by the woman who has organized a corps she calls the Leales, the Loyal Ones, drilled from manuals he himself supplies. He folds the republiqueta's forces into his order of battle. Juana is no longer an irregular; she is an officer of the Army of the North in fact, if not yet in commission.
suggested_refs: The Casa Real de Moneda, Potosí, Belgrano's headquarters in the Villa Imperial
sources: juana_azurduy.journey.json research; belgrano.journey.json (Potosí headquarters, shared pin)

stops.name: Pampa de Vilcapugio, the battle lost while winning
stops.campa: On the high plateau of Vilcapugio, Belgrano's army breaks Pezuela's center and believes the day won, only for a false report of retreat and a collapse of the reserve to turn triumph into rout within the hour. Juana's Leales, posted to the flank, hold their ground longer than most and cover the disordered withdrawal of units that panic before they do. She sees, in the space of an afternoon, how quickly a battle already won can be lost to confusion rather than to the enemy, a lesson she will not forget in the guerrilla war she returns to fight on her own ground.
suggested_refs: The pampa of Vilcapugio, Potosí department, where Belgrano's Second Expedition first breaks

stops.name: Ayohúma, the Leales and the sabre of Belgrano
stops.campa: On the plain of Ayohúma, whose old name means head of the dead, Pezuela's guns dominate from the heights and the rebuilt patriot army is broken a second time. Juana commands the right flank with her Battalion of the Leales under Cornelio Zelaya, and holds it under fire alongside María Remedios del Valle, the Black captain the soldiers already call Madre de la Patria. The army is lost, but Belgrano, watching the two women's companies fight to the last order, does not forget it: for this day, and for Ayohúma's discipline in ruin, he will within three years give Juana the sabre that carried him through Salta, Tucumán, and the Jujuy exodus.
suggested_refs: Belgrano's personal sabre, later placed in Juana's hands, kept afterward in her wooden box of relics
María Remedios del Valle iconography (shared figure, belgrano.journey.json)

stops.name: Chuquisaca province, the ruse against Carvallo
stops.campa: Carvallo, a royalist official under the notorious Sánchez de Velasco, has made a trade of extorting and executing indigenous villagers across the province. Padilla and the guerrilla chief José Ignacio Zárate capture Sánchez de Velasco outright; when royalist troops seize Padilla and Zárate in reprisal and begin to torture them, Juana and Huallparrimachi save them by cunning rather than force, shouting Zárate's feared name through the dark until the drunk, panicked guards believe his whole company has returned and abandon the prisoners rather than face him. Padilla and Zárate walk free before dawn, saved by two voices in the dark.
suggested_refs: The republiqueta's tactic of psychological warfare against isolated royalist garrisons

stops.name: Cerro de las Carretas, the death of Huallparrimachi
stops.campa: A bribed guide leads royalist Colonel Sebastián Benavente to the guerrilla camp at Cerro de las Carretas, two leagues from Tarabuco, and three days of fighting follow among the crags. In the worst of it a cannon-shot aimed at Juana is intercepted by Huallparrimachi's own body; he throws himself into its path and dies of the wound, the poet-lieutenant she had raised as a son given for the mother who raised him. The camp holds the ground despite the loss, and the action draws new recruits to the republiqueta even as it costs Juana one of the people she loved best in the war.
suggested_refs: Juan Huallparrimachi's grave near Cerro de las Carretas, and his surviving Quechua poems

stops.name: Valle de Segura, the deaths of the children
stops.campa: In the fever-ridden lowlands of the Valle de Segura, where the republiqueta shelters its noncombatants, malaria moves through the Padilla children one by one. Juana buries her sons Manuel and Mariano herself, in graves she cannot mark for fear of desecration, and rides to recover Juliana and Mercedes from royalist hands only to watch the same fever take them within days of the rescue. Four of her five children die this way, camp-born and camp-buried, casualties the official histories of battles never count. Afterward those who serve under her say she no longer spares a captured officer as she once did.
suggested_refs: The unmarked graves of the Valle de Segura, kept unrecorded by the mother who dug them

stops.name: Pintatora, birth in the field and the captured standard
stops.campa: The labor pains come on Juana at Pintatora with the sound of royalist cavalry already entering the camp; she gives birth to her fifth child, Luisa, within earshot of the alarm, by the bank of the Río Grande, in the ordinary violence of a guerrilla republic that keeps no separate peace for mothers. Hours later, the canon says, she is back among her troops, rallying the line and personally cutting down the standard-bearer of the retreating royalist company. Luisa will be the only one of the five children to outlive the war, carried through it in a saddle-basket while her mother fights.
suggested_refs: Luisa Padilla y Azurduy, the sole surviving child, born at Pintatora

segments.name: El Villar, Cerro Rico, and the Teniente Coronel

stops.name: El Villar, the standard of La Hera
stops.campa: Leading thirty mounted fighters, several of them women of her own recruiting whom the countryside has taken to calling the Amazonas, Juana charges the forces of the Spanish general La Hera near El Villar and breaks them, capturing the royal standard with her own hand and recovering a store of muskets the republiqueta badly needs. The action is small in numbers and enormous in what it proves: that a column she personally leads, not merely organizes from the rear, can take a fortified position from regular Spanish troops. Five days later she will ride on to prove it again at Potosí's own mountain.
suggested_refs: The captured royal standard of El Villar, forwarded to Buenos Aires as proof of the victory

stops.name: Cerro Rico de Potosí, the assault on the silver mountain
stops.campa: Five days after El Villar, Juana leads a cavalry strike against the fortifications thrown up around the Cerro Rico itself, the cone-shaped mountain whose silver has paid for the entire Spanish empire's wars for three centuries. Her riders take the outer defenses and another royalist standard before withdrawing; the raid cannot hold the mountain, but it plants the republiqueta's flag, briefly, on the most valuable piece of ground in South America, within sight of the Casa de Moneda's own chimneys. Reports of the action, and of El Villar before it, are what finally reach Buenos Aires and change how Pueyrredón's government rates her.
suggested_refs: The Cerro Rico de Potosí, the mountain that funded the Spanish Empire, briefly under her flag

stops.name: La Laguna, the commission and Belgrano's sabre delivered
stops.campa: A courier reaches the camp at La Laguna carrying the decree Juan Martín de Pueyrredón, Director Supremo of the United Provinces, has signed on 13 August 1816: Juana Azurduy, teniente coronel, commanding a division to be called the Decididos del Perú, entitled to wear the uniform of the rank. With the commission comes something Belgrano chooses to send in place of the standard-issue blade, his own personal sabre, the one that rode with him through Salta, Tucumán, and the Jujuy exodus and stood beside her at broken Ayohúma. It is the highest rank yet given a woman in the armies of the revolution.
suggested_refs: The decree of 13 August 1816 and Belgrano's sabre, both preserved afterward in her wooden document box

segments.name: La Laguna: the Death of Padilla

stops.name: La Laguna, the Battle of La Laguna
stops.campa: Fresh from a victory at Tinteros, Padilla learns of a coordinated royalist advance: two thousand men under Miguel Tacón from Chuquisaca, seven hundred under Francisco Javier de Aguilera from Vallegrande. He splits his force, ordering infantry to meet Aguilera head-on while cavalry under Cueto strikes the rear; the plan misfires when Aguilera's rearguard holds and Padilla's line falls back in disorder toward La Laguna. It is not yet the disaster it will become within a day, but the republiqueta, victorious so many times in fifteen places across this province, has never before been caught between two royalist columns at once.
suggested_refs: The pass at Tinteros, site of the victory that preceded the disaster

stops.name: El Villar, the death and the pike
stops.campa: Padilla regroups at the sanctuary of El Villar; Aguilera, trailing him unseen, launches a surprise cavalry raid the next morning. Juana, commanding the reserve with the treasury and the arms, takes two gunshot wounds, leg and chest, and fights on through the pain to hold the line. Padilla is shot from his horse and, by the most repeated account, beheaded where he falls; Aguilera mounts his head on a pike in the plaza of El Villar, and beside it, by mistake, the head of a woman fighter he takes for Juana herself. She learns of her widowhood still bleeding, on the road, and has to be kept by her own men from riding back to die at his side.
suggested_refs: The plaza of El Villar, today Villa Serrano, where the heads were displayed
Manuel Ovando's 1882 deposition, an alternate eyewitness account of Padilla's death

stops.name: Valle de Segura, the treasury, Luisa, and the vow
stops.campa: Wounded and widowed within the same day, Juana does not stop to grieve where she is told the grief is safe. She rides for the Valle de Segura to secure what remains of the republiqueta's treasury, some sixty thousand duros, her one surviving daughter Luisa, and the documents that hold her own commission as teniente coronel, prizes she judges the war cannot afford to lose along with her husband. Over his unmarked grave, later, she will swear the vow her own hand records for the government: to avenge his death and to go on living by his example, whatever it costs her.
stops.quote: Only the sacred love of my country has made bearable the loss of a husband over whose grave I swore to avenge his death and follow his example.
stops.quote_source: Letter to the government, cited in Argentine historiography (El Historiador; correspondence archives, 1810s-1820s)
suggested_refs: Luisa Padilla y Azurduy, saved from the rout at nine months old

stops.name: La Laguna, the recovery of Padilla's head
stops.campa: Juana sends the recruiter Caipé through the villages to raise a hundred indigenous volunteers and a hundred women fighters, and leads them back against Colonel Francisco Baruri's garrison at La Laguna in what the histories of the war call its cruelest reprisal: every royalist soldier found is killed. Padilla's head, weeks on its pike, maggot-infested and picked over by crows, is taken down and brought to a church altar to be given the honors owed a colonel of the republic. It is not peace. It is the only mercy the war still has to offer a widow who buried four children before she buried, in pieces, her husband.
suggested_refs: The church at La Laguna where Padilla's remains received ecclesiastical honors

segments.name: Salta and the Years with Güemes

stops.name: La Laguna, the council of caudillos
stops.campa: With Padilla dead the republiqueta's captains gather in council and, unusually for the age, elect Juana herself to preside over the choice of his successor; she names Jacinto Cueto commander, with Esteban Fernández as his second. The unity does not hold. Apolinar Zárate and others break away, some drawn as much by the recovered treasury as by any quarrel of strategy, and the republiqueta that fought as one body under the Padillas begins to fragment into rival bands. Juana, widowed, wounded, and outranking every man in the room by commission if not by vote, watches fifteen years of shared war start to come apart in a single meeting.
suggested_refs: The council of caudillos at La Laguna, an unusual instance of a woman presiding over a war council's succession

stops.name: Salta, joining Martín Miguel de Güemes
stops.campa: As the republiqueta splinters behind her, Juana sends word south by the friar José Indalecio de Salazar to Martín Miguel de Güemes, the gaucho commander who has made Salta into the shield that keeps the royalists from ever again reaching Tucumán. Güemes receives her with the honor her commission is owed, appoints a successor to Padilla's command whom the local chiefs will not accept, and takes Juana herself into the irregular war he is fighting along the Salta-Jujuy frontier: the gaucho partisan bands, the same tactics of ambush and vanishing that she perfected in Chuquisaca's ravines, now practiced on the southern edge of the same war.
suggested_refs: The gaucho war of Salta and Jujuy under Martín Miguel de Güemes

stops.name: The Salta-Jujuy frontier, the gaucho war
stops.campa: For three years Juana rides the borderland between Salta and Jujuy as one of Güemes's officers, part of a partisan war fought without pitched battles: ambush the royalist patrol, vanish into the quebradas, let the mountains do the work regular armies cannot. The relationship between the widowed colonel and the gaucho general grows, by the account both contemporaries and later historians credit, into something more than command and subordinate, though neither leaves a record plain enough to settle it. What is certain is that for these years she has, for the first time since Padilla's death, a war whose commander she trusts absolutely.
suggested_refs: The quebradas of the Salta-Jujuy frontier, terrain of the gaucho partisan war

stops.name: Salta, the death of Güemes
stops.campa: A royalist raiding party surprises Güemes outside Salta on the night of 7 June 1821; he is shot and dies of the wound on the seventeenth, the last great guerrilla commander of the northern war gone within days of the injury. For Juana the loss closes a chapter she cannot reopen: her military career, in any effective sense, ends with his. Without Güemes's protection and without a republiqueta left whole enough to command, she is a teniente coronel and later coronel of an army that no longer has a northern front to give her, and the long decline into poverty begins here, not later.
suggested_refs: The Monumento a Güemes, Salta, commemorating the general whose death ends her active command

segments.name: The Return, Bolívar's Visit, and the Common Grave

stops.name: Chuquisaca, return and the memorial to the government
stops.campa: With the Spanish withdrawal from Upper Peru all but complete, Juana returns after nearly a decade away to a Chuquisaca now calling itself Sucre, bringing eleven-year-old Luisa and little else. No one in the city greets her; the caudillos who could vouch for her service are scattered or dead, and the new administration owes her nothing it has yet chosen to pay. She writes to the government the memorial that will define the rest of her life, asking not for charity but for what the law itself allows a widow and an officer: her husband's pension, and the salary of her own rank.
stops.quote: The enjoyment of my late husband's widow's pension, and the salary that may correspond to my own rank.
stops.quote_source: Memorial to the Bolivian government, 1825, cited in Argentine and Bolivian biographical accounts
suggested_refs: Juana's 1825 memorial to the government, first document of her decades-long pension struggle

stops.name: Chuquisaca, the visit of Bolívar and Sucre
stops.campa: In the days after Chuquisaca votes itself the capital of the republic that will bear his name, Simón Bolívar, with Antonio José de Sucre at his side, calls on Juana in person, an honor he pays almost no one else in the new state. He grants her a pension of sixty pesos, the rank of coronel, and, to the officers around him, the sentence that will outlast every honor Upper Peru gives her in her lifetime: that this country should not be called Bolivia after his own name, but Padilla or Azurduy, since it was they who made it free. Sucre will later raise the pension to a hundred pesos.
suggested_refs: Casa de la Libertad, Sucre, where the republic naming itself for Bolívar receives the woman he says it should be named for instead
sources: bolivar.journey.json (Chuquisaca, the republic that bears his name, shared pin, 1825-11-03)

stops.name: Cullco, the hacienda restored, the letter to Manuela Sáenz
stops.campa: Of all the Azurduy and Padilla properties confiscated across fifteen years of war, the government recognizes her claim to only one, the hacienda of Cullco, which poverty will eventually force her to sell for far less than its worth. From there, on 15 December 1825, newly confirmed coronel, she writes to Manuela Sáenz, herself a colonel and Bolívar's companion, a letter of restrained feeling: gratitude for the rank, discomfort at seeing former royalist officers now serving beside the victors, and grief, plainly stated and without bitterness, for the comrades and the women fighters who did not live to see this recognition arrive.
suggested_refs: The Azurduy-Sáenz correspondence of December 1825, two women colonels of the independence wars writing to each other

stops.name: Sucre, the pension cut, decades of poverty
stops.campa: Bolívar's pension, already reduced by successive administrations that treat Upper Peru's war debts as someone else's to honor, is cancelled outright in 1857 under President José María Linares. Buenos Aires, for its part, has long since decided the Alto Perú campaigns are a foreign country's history and owes her nothing. Her sister Rosalía controls what family property remains; Luisa marries and moves away. Juana, alone, takes in a crippled orphan boy, Indalecio Sandi, and raises him on almost nothing, the same instinct that once made her a mother to Huallparrimachi turned now toward a stranger's child in her own old age.
suggested_refs: The pension revocation of 1857 under President José María Linares

stops.name: Sucre, the Coripata tambo, the box with the sabre
stops.campa: In her last years Juana lives in a whitewashed room off a travelers' inn in the Coripata quarter of Sucre, walls of adobe, beams gnawed by rats, a bed of native cane matting. The historian Gabriel René Moreno and others who seek her out find an old woman who says little and keeps, within reach, a small wooden box holding Belgrano's sabre, her commission as teniente coronel, and her medals, the whole of her rank reduced to what fits in a single chest. To those who ask how she bears it she is remembered saying only that the one thing left to leave her daughter is her tears.
stops.quote: The only thing I can leave my daughter are my tears.
stops.quote_source: Popular tradition, widely cited in Argentine and Bolivian biographical accounts of her final years
suggested_refs: The wooden box holding Belgrano's sabre, her commission, and her medals, her only remaining estate

stops.name: Sucre, death in the common grave
stops.campa: Juana dies on 25 May 1862, eighty-one years old, in the small rented room where Indalecio Sandi has kept her company on a cot of his own. Sandi carries word to the military authorities and asks for the funeral honors due a coronel of the republic; Major Joaquín Taborga turns him away, the garrison being occupied that day with the festivities of Independence Day, the anniversary of the revolution she helped begin at Chuquisaca fifty-three years before. She is buried in the town cemetery in a common grave, a priest's brief prayer the whole of the ceremony, the cost of the burial one peso.
suggested_refs: The common grave of the cemetery of Sucre, unmarked until Indalecio Sandi's old-age testimony located it decades later
Cueca 'Juana Azurduy' (Félix Luna / Ariel Ramírez), sung by Mercedes Sosa, the song that carries her name into the twentieth century
